content/docs/sem3/csi247/collections/ind: --- title: Java Collections Framework description: Visual study map for Lists, Sets, Maps, and the Java Collections hierarchy. --- # Java Collections Framework Last Updated: July 11, 2026 This comprehensive visual map covers the Java Collections Framework, including: - **Core Interfaces:** Iterable, Collection, List, Set, and Map hierarchies. - **List Implementations:** ArrayList (dynamic arrays) vs. LinkedList (doubly-linked nodes). - **Set Implementations:** HashSet (hash tables), TreeSet (Red-Black trees), and LinkedHashSet. - **Map Implementations:** HashMap, TreeMap, and ConcurrentHashMap for thread safety. - **Utilities:** Iterators, Comparators, and the Collections utility class.
content/docs/sem3/csi247/collections/que: --- title: Collections Practice Questions description: Exam-style questions on the Java Collections Framework. --- # Practice Questions: Collections Explain how HashMap handles collisions in Java 8+. What is the threshold for treeification? [5]} solution={<>It uses separate chaining with linked lists. If a bucket exceeds 8 nodes (and total capacity >= 64), it converts the list to a Red-Black Tree to improve worst-case lookup from O(N) to O(log N).} /> What happens if you use a mutable object as a key in a HashMap, and then mutate it after insertion? [5]} solution={<>The object's hashCode changes. When you try to retrieve it, the HashMap looks in the wrong bucket, and the entry is effectively lost (memory leak).} /> You need to implement a queue that frequently adds to the tail and removes from the head. Which is better: ArrayList or LinkedList? Justify with Big-O. [4]} solution={<>LinkedList is better. Adding to tail is O(1) (if tail pointer is maintained) and removing from head is O(1). ArrayList requires O(N) to shift elements when removing from the head.} /> Why does ArrayList generally outperform LinkedList in real-world iteration, despite both being O(N)? [4]} solution={<>CPU Cache Locality. ArrayList uses a contiguous backing array, which is highly cache-friendly. LinkedList nodes are scattered in heap memory, causing frequent cache misses.} />

content/docs/sem3/csi247/heaps-and-prior: --- title: Heaps & Priority Queues description: Visual study map for Binary Heaps, Heapify, and Priority Queue applications. --- # Heaps & Priority Queues Last Updated: July 11, 2026 This comprehensive visual map covers Heaps and Priority Queues, including: - **Binary Heaps:** Min-Heap and Max-Heap properties and array-based representations. - **Core Operations:** Insert (Heapify-Up), Extract-Min/Max (Heapify-Down), and Peek. - **Build Heap:** The O(N) algorithm to convert an arbitrary array into a valid heap. - **Applications:** Priority Queues, Dijkstra's Algorithm, Top-K elements, and Heap Sort.

--- title: Heaps Practice Questions description: Exam-style questions on Heaps and Priority Queues. --- # Practice Questions: Heaps Given a 0-indexed array representing a Min-Heap, write the formulas to find the parent, left child, and right child of an element at index i. [3]} solution={<>Parent: (i-1)/2. Left Child: 2i+1. Right Child: 2i+2.} /> Why is the time complexity of buildHeap (heapifying an entire array) O(N) and not O(N log N)? [5]} solution={<>Most nodes are at the bottom of the tree and require 0 or 1 swaps. The mathematical sum of the heights of all nodes in a complete binary tree converges to O(N), not N * log(N).} /> Write an algorithm to find the K largest elements in a stream of N numbers. What data structure do you use and what is the time complexity? [6]} solution={<>Use a Min-Heap of size K. Iterate through the N numbers. If the heap size < K, push. If the number is greater than the heap's root (min), pop the root and push the new number. Time: O(N log K).} /> Why use a Min-Heap of size K instead of a Max-Heap of size N to find the K largest elements? [4]} solution={<>A Min-Heap of size K keeps the smallest of the 'top K' elements at the root, allowing O(1) comparisons and O(log K) evictions. A Max-Heap of size N would require O(N) to build and O(K log N) to extract, which is much slower for large N and small K.} />

# Practice Questions: Graphs

<ExamQuestion title="Question 1: Dijkstra vs Bellman-Ford [10 Marks]">
  <SubQuestion part="a" prompt={<>Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail on graphs with negative edge weights? [4]</>} solution={<>Dijkstra's relies on a greedy assumption: once a node is popped from the priority queue, its shortest path is finalized. Negative edges can later provide a shorter path to an already 'finalized' node, breaking the algorithm.</>} />
  <SubQuestion part="b" prompt={<>How does Bellman-Ford detect a negative weight cycle? [6]</>} solution={<>It relaxes all edges V-1 times. If on the V-th iteration, any edge can still be relaxed (distance updates), it proves a negative weight cycle exists, as a valid shortest path can have at most V-1 edges.</>} />
</ExamQuestion>

<ExamQuestion title="Question 2: Topological Sort [8 Marks]">
  <SubQuestion part="a" prompt={<>Explain Kahn's Algorithm for Topological Sorting. What data structure is primarily used? [5]</>} solution={<>Calculate in-degrees for all nodes. Push all nodes with in-degree 0 into a Queue. Pop a node, add to result, and decrement in-degrees of its neighbors. If a neighbor's in-degree becomes 0, push to Queue.</>} />
  <SubQuestion part="b" prompt={<>How do you use Kahn's Algorithm to detect if a graph contains a cycle? [3]</>} solution={<>If the final topological order array contains fewer nodes than the total vertices in the graph (V), it means some nodes were trapped in a cycle and never reached an in-degree of 0.</>} />
</ExamQuestion>
